items.title: Three correct answers to one question about one property
items.summary: What four US county property systems taught me about building an Apify Actor an AI agent can trust. The Cook County assessor mailed a value of 3,041 for parcel 17052170040000. The assessor certified 3,041. The Board of Review cut it to 1,303. Same parcel, same year, three numbers, 57% apart, and all three are correct. Which one answers "what is this assessed at" depends on where in the appeal cycle you were standing when you asked, and nothing in the number says which one you have. There is a second trap in the same field. Illinois assesses residential property at a fraction of market value, roughly 10%, so 3,041 is not a $3,041 property and 1,303 is not a $1,303 one. The number is a step in a tax calculation, never a price. I asked the same question seventeen hundred miles away. Parcel 3532803300, a house on Ridgegate Row in La Jolla, came back at 2,022,509. That is a Proposition 13 factored base year value: what the property was worth when it last changed hands, grown by at most 2% a year since. items.title: Demystifying Abstract Syntax Trees: How Code Becomes Action in Node.js
items.summary: What is an Abstract Syntax Tree? An Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) is a structured, tree-like representation of source code written in a programming language. Instead of treating code as a flat string of plain text characters, a computer breaks it down into an interconnected tree of nodes. Each node represents a specific construct in the code, such as a variable declaration, a function call, or a mathematical operator. By converting raw text into this tree structure, compilers, interpreters, and developer tools can programmatically inspect, analyze, and transform source code. If you ever did sentence diagramming in school grammar class, you already understand how an Abstract Syntax Tree works. Imagine taking the sentence: "The smart developer writes clean code." To a computer reading plain text, that sentence is just 38 individual characters including spaces. It has no inherent structure. But when a human parses it, we break it down into grammatical components: Sentence Subject (Noun Phrase): "The smart developer" Article: "The" Adjective: "smart" Noun: "developer" Predicate (Verb Phrase): "writes clean code" Verb: "writes" Direct Object (Noun Phrase): "clean code" Adjective: "clean" N

items.summary: For most businesses in 2026, a cross-platform app built with Flutter or React Native is the sensible starting point. It usually cuts upfront cost by roughly a third compared with building separate iOS and Android apps, and the performance gap now matters only for a narrow set of products, such as games, heavy animation or apps that lean on very new hardware features. Native still wins when raw speed is the product. Everything else is a question of scope, not technology. That answer sounds tidy, but it hides the decisions that actually sink app projects: unclear scope, a rushed first release and no plan for what happens after launch. This guide walks through each of them. Why so many apps fail before they ship Ask a founder what went wrong with an app that never found users and the story is rarely about code. It is usually one of three things. The feature list kept growing while the launch date stayed fixed. Nobody tested the idea with real customers before the build began. Or the budget covered development but nothing for the year that follows, when bugs surface, operating systems update and users ask for changes. Prisma ORM removed its Rust query engine in version 7, released in November 2025, in favour of a TypeScript/WebAssembly "query compiler" that talks to your database through a JavaScript driver adapter instead of a native binary. I tried Blazor more than once, because I wanted one platform from the database to the browser. Each time a project needed a modern, highly customized interface, I ended up reaching for React and its component ecosystem again. So I started building the components I was missing, in Blazor, with the look and the developer experience I was used to. That work became RaxUI. RaxUI is a set of 68 open-source components for Blazor and React that share one theme. A CLI copies each component's source into your app, so you own the code and can change any of it. Your code, not a dependency. raxui add copies .razor files and their CSS into your project. Installed components run without the CLI, and there is no runtime package to upgrade. items.summary: When Notifio finds a listing that was not on a rental search page the last time it looked, four things happen. A line goes into the activity log, a row goes into the recent-finds list, a native desktop banner appears, and our server sends an email. Exactly one of those four can be turned off, and the route that does it carries the policy in a comment: /** * Local alert channels. items.title: Five of our eight delete routes delete something you did not ask them to
items.summary: Notifio watches rental search pages from the user's own machine, so most of what it knows is on their disk rather than our server. Its renderer is a React UI that talks to a local Express server over 127.0.0.1, and eight of that server's routes destroy something. items.title: 61% of our HTML is inside script tags. Then I compressed it and found the real bill.
items.summary: I crawled all 38 pages of notifio.app to count internal links, which turned into its own post. While the HTML was sitting in a directory I measured something else: how much of it is actually HTML. 38 pages total 2,142,883 bytes (2.04 MiB) inside 1,315,784 bytes (61.4%) RSC flight payload 1,184,338 bytes (55.3%) JSON-LD 106,700 bytes ( 5.0%) everything else 24,746 bytes ( 1.2%) Sixty one percent. The thing a browser parses as markup is the minority of the document on every single page. This is a Next.js App Router site, so each response carries the React Server Components payload: the serialised tree the client runtime uses to hydrate, and to render a client-side navigation without a round trip. It arrives as a sequence of self.__next_f.push(...) calls at the end of the body. Our pages have between 4 and 22 of them. The payload is not a summary of the page. It contains the text. Pick any sentence off a page and count it in the source: curl -s https://notifio.app/alerts/kamernet | grep -c "Kamernet lets you save a search" # 2 Two hits, 28 KB apart in the document: one in the markup, one inside a . items.title: RAG Pipeline Utils v3.8: Testing RAG Answers in TypeScript
items.summary: v3.8.0 is about testing RAG in TypeScript. The answer matchers now compile with types, and a new guide walks through the whole setup with Vitest, from a unit test to a test set that fails CI when answers get worse. Nothing breaks for existing code. npm install @devilsdev/rag-pipeline-utils@^3.8.0 @devilsdev/rag-pipeline-utils/testing has had three matchers for a while: toBeGroundedIn (every sentence of the answer is supported by its sources, numbers and negation included), toCite and toContainNoPII. They worked in JavaScript. In TypeScript, expect(result).toBeGroundedIn() didn't compile, because nothing told TypeScript the matchers existed. Worse, the declaration our own Testing page suggested failed under Vitest 5 with "All declarations of 'Assertion' must have identical type parameters". 3.8.0 exports their signatures as RagMatchers. Add them to Vitest's Matchers once, in a declaration file: import "vitest"; import type { RagMatchers } from "@devilsdev/rag-pipeline-utils/testing"; declare module "vitest" { interface Matchers extends RagMatchers {} } Now the matchers type-check like any other assertion. items.title: MCP Explained Simply: How to Build a Claude‑Powered AI Agent with AWS Lambda
items.summary: Ever wondered how Claude can keep context across dozens of calls without re‑sending the whole prompt each time? The Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes that possible, and you can host it in a serverless Lambda in minutes. Let’s demystify the wire‑format and see a real implementation. When you talk to a large language model (LLM) like Claude, you normally send a big text block that contains everything the model needs to remember: the system prompt, user messages, and any prior assistant replies. This works, but it wastes bandwidth and token budget when the conversation grows long. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, is a lightweight way to tell the model “here is the next piece of the conversation, and here’s the token that represents everything that came before.” Instead of re‑sending the whole history, you send a small session token that the model expands internally. In plain English: MCP is like handing a librarian a library card (the token) instead of re‑handing the entire stack of books every time you ask for the next chapter. Why care about this? items.title: 4 KB of Text Was Holding 200 MB of Memory
items.summary: kept: 200 strings, 3.9 KB of text heap: +200.0 MB That's the output of a small test, and the two lines should not be able to coexist. An array holds 200 short IDs, about 4 KB of characters. Forcing a full garbage collection doesn't help. The heap stays 200 MB bigger. Picture the same thing in a Node service. Each request carries a large JSON body, and you keep only its ID in a Map for later. The body goes out of scope immediately, so it should be gone. Instead, memory climbs by the size of a request body, every request, until the process dies. Every memory leak guide says the same thing: something still references your object. So you look for it. A closure capturing the body? A logger buffering requests? A forgotten listener? items.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
items.summary: I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock. So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted. DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all. The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero. I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. items.title: I Expected a 100x JSON Slowdown. I Got 1.9x.
items.summary: I had a little serialize helper that sailed through code review. It looked like this: return JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { ... }). A fresh options object, built right there in the method, on every call. items.title: Stop Hand-Rolling JSON Lines With WriteLine. .NET 11 Writes Them for You
items.summary: TL;DR: JsonSerializer.SerializeAsyncEnumerable(stream, items, topLevelValues: true) writes canonical JSON Lines: one compact value per line, LF after every one. No more WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serialize(x)) loops. This ships in .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license, but is not GA yet. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. JSON Lines (JSONL) is one JSON value per line. It is the format of choice for log files, data exports, and anything you want to append to without rewriting the whole file. System.Text.Json could already read it. On .NET 10, DeserializeAsyncEnumerable(stream, topLevelValues: true) streams top-level values just fine. Writing it was on you: await using var writer = new StreamWriter("orders.jsonl"); await foreach (var order in LoadOrders()) { await writer.WriteLineAsync(JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, options)); } It works until someone reuses an options with WriteIndented = true. items.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
items.summary: "OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use.

items.summary: A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports: Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes. items.title: Return template
items.summary: Introduction A well-structured web application should keep presentation and application logic separate. The View should primarily describe the HTML structure, while server-side code handles data processing and application behavior. CodeBehind is a .NET Core framework built around this separation. Unlike approaches that embed server-side logic directly into HTML, CodeBehind provides mechanisms for keeping the View focused on presentation. However, loops and conditional statements can make this separation difficult to maintain. Consider a navigation menu generated from a collection of pages. In Razor, the implementation might look like this: @foreach (var page in Model.Pages) { @page.Title } Although this syntax is convenient, the View now contains both HTML and server-side control flow. items.title: Working with templates in View
items.summary: Introduction As web applications grow, maintaining repeated HTML structures across multiple pages can become a challenge. Page headers, product cards, information panels, and other common elements often share the same markup. Copying these structures into every view increases duplication and makes future changes more difficult. CodeBehind addresses this through its Template system. It allows developers to define reusable sections of a page and insert them into other parts of the view. Templates can be defined directly inside a page or stored in external files. Both Razor Syntax and Standard Syntax are supported. Consider an online store where several pages display product information using the same HTML structure. Instead of repeating the markup for every product, we can define a template named ProductCard. Here is an example using Razor Syntax: @#ProductCard{ @model.ProductName @model.ProductDescription @model.ProductPrice } The template can then be referenced wherever its content is needed: @#ProductCard When CodeBehind processes the page, the template reference is replaced with the content defined in ProductCard. items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Building Subscriptions Without Storing a Single Card Number
items.summary: We just added recurring product subscriptions to StoreFlux (a headless commerce backend), and the design decision I want to write about is the one that felt obvious in hindsight but wasn't the first thing I reached for: we don't store a customer's card at all. The "normal" way to build subscriptions is to tokenize the customer's card on the gateway (Stripe customer + payment method, say), save that token, and on each billing date fire an off-session charge against it. That's a completely reasonable design. It's also one most commerce platforms already have sitting around, because it's the obvious answer. I didn't want to build that, for a fairly unglamorous reason: it's a second payment path. Checkout already has a payment path — tested, handles declines, handles 3D Secure challenges, handles webhooks, handles every gateway-specific weirdness we've already run into. A separate off-session billing path duplicates all of that, badly, because off-session charges can't show the customer a 3DS challenge if one gets triggered. items.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader bbsguru shares a report from KrebsOnSecurity: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into "free" mobile and desktop applications. items.title: Discord Is Ditching Electron For Rust
items.summary: Discord is replacing Electron with a desktop client built fully in Rust, which the company says should significantly reduce the app's notoriously high resource usage while improving performance and memory safety. "We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there," explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. "That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust." The Verge reports: Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app. It's not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company "hope to get it into testing with users soon." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. Everything that cached its width at first layout was wrong after the first fold. containerRelativeFrame across the fold My page views used containerRelativeFrame(.horizontal) for carou

items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. items.title: Opening a panel right under the text caret on macOS
items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.
